orders.rationale: A gets the main fact wrong: Barack Obama, not Trump, was president for all of 2016. Its own text even says Trump served from 2017, so it contradicts itself. B is correct and explains that Trump won the 2016 election but took office in 2017. B is clear and backed by its source.

A is right: Obama was president for all of 2016, and Trump won the election that year but only took office in January 2017. B wrongly names Trump as the 2016 president, and its own claim that he served from 2017 contradicts that. B's cited sources don't support its claim, so its grounding is poor.

A wrongly treats 'Joseph B. Strauss' as a separate contributor and leaves out Ellis and Morrow. B accurately describes the team: Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis (credited in 2007), Morrow and Paine, with correct dates. B is more accurate and complete and is well sourced.

A is accurate and gives the full team: Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis, Morrow and Paine, with the context. B lists "Joseph B. Strauss" as a separate contributor when he's the same person, leaves out Ellis and Morrow, and overstates Strauss's role as primary designer. A is clearly better.

B explains Rayleigh scattering, why the sky isn't green, and why it isn't violet. Its "10 times more" figure is too high: blue vs red is about 5–6×, and the ~10× figure fits violet vs red. A is correct on the basics but never really explains why the sky isn't green, and it leans on a student journal as a source.

A answers "why not green" directly and accurately. It explains that scattering rises toward shorter wavelengths with no peak at green, then covers violet and how our cones respond. Its ozone claim is slightly shaky but minor. B only explains why the sky is blue. Its "rather than green" conclusion doesn't follow from its reasoning, and its wording about red light is odd.

A is correct but thin. Its "magnets create field through winding" line is vague and it doesn't explain why the motor keeps rotating. B explains the Lorentz force, how the commutator keeps a DC motor turning, and the brushless and induction variants, and it notes combustion engines. B is clearer and more complete. B's sources look relevant to its claims; A cites [2], [3] and [6] but never uses them.

Answer A is accurate. It explains how the Lorentz force turns the shaft, then covers the commutator, brushless motors and induction motors, and it points out that combustion engines work differently. Its claims fit the sources it cites. Answer B is also correct and covers both kinds of motor, but it is too thin to explain how either one actually works.

B is accurate and covers more: snout, teeth, salt glands, habitat, range and color. Its sources match its claims. A is correct on families and snout shape but too thin. Both answers are accurate. A explains acid activation, double-acting powder, when recipes use both, and why you can't swap them one-for-one, all clearly and practically. B is correct but thin: it skips double-acting powder, substitution, and practical tips. A is more complete and more useful.

Both answers say espresso has more caffeine per ounce but drip has more per serving. A mixes up its serving sizes (200 mL vs 240 mL) and is wordy. B is clearer and more complete: it adds the double-shot comparison and notes that amounts vary by bean, roast and brew. Its figures are plausible and backed by its sources.

A is better because it gives per-ounce numbers, covers the double shot, and notes that amounts vary. It's also clear on a phone. B is correct but repeats itself, mixes 200 mL and 240 mL servings, and lists sources it never uses.

Both answers are correct: the Danube flows through Budapest and into the Black Sea. B's extra facts are accurate and supported by its sources. These are the river's ~28 km through Budapest, its ~2,850 km length across ten countries, and the delta on the Romania–Ukraine border. The delta detail adds to the "where does it end up" part. A is correct but bare and cites generic sources. B is slightly better.

Both answers correctly name the Danube and the Black Sea. A adds accurate context (Buda and Pest, the Black Forest source, the delta on the Romania–Ukraine border) and cites specific sources. B gets the facts right but is bare, and its sources are vague labels. A is slightly better and still short.

It also wrongly says the question contains an error, and its George VI citation doesn't support the answer, so it's confusing. Answer B is correct, clear and well sourced: Victoria, 31 March 1889, and accurate reign details.

B is correct: Berners-Lee went to Oxford (The Queen's College) and earned a first-class physics degree, and the extra details are accurate. A never names Oxford and lists Emanuel School, a secondary school, as if it were part of the answer. That is misleading and leaves the question only partly answered.

A correctly names Queen's College, Oxford (1973–76, first-class physics) and adds accurate details. B never says "Oxford" and lists Emanuel School, which is a secondary school, not a university. That is misleading. B also cites several sources it doesn't use, and its answer is vaguer.

Both answers correctly name the Cambodian riel. A is right but bare, and its listed sources (Angkor pages, a Phnom Penh hotel listing) are weak support for a currency claim. B adds accurate, useful context with relevant sources: the dollar is widely used, the exchange rate is about 4,000 riel to the dollar, and riel is used for small change. That suits a traveller.

Both correctly name Cambodia and the riel. A adds accurate, practical context that matters to visitors: US dollars are widely used, the riel trades at about 4,000 to the dollar, and riel is given as change. Its sources fit its claims. B is correct but thin, and its cited Angkor pages probably don't support the currency claim.

Both correctly say about 1.3 million Earths by volume. B goes further: it explains the 109³ scaling, and it notes that solid spheres can't fill space completely, which gives about 960,000 intact Earths at 74% packing. That math is right. A is accurate but brief, and its line separating volume from diameter adds little. B is more complete and more useful.

Both answers correctly give about 1.3 million Earths by volume. A also explains why: the Sun is about 109 times Earth's diameter, and volume scales with the cube of that. It adds the sphere-packing caveat that only about 960,000 whole Earths would fit, which matches its cited BBC source. B is correct but thin, and its sources are generic.

Both get ~4,043 m right from 8,848.86 and 4,805.59. A also explains that Mont Blanc's height changes, says it couldn't find an official 2025 figure, and gives a sourced range. B is correct but repeats the question as filler, and its sources are vague. A is clearer about what it knows.
